title: Component contract (framework-agnostic)
description:
Describes ONE component completely enough to build it, in any framework. The reasoning is in contracts/README.md.

This file lives at contracts/ rather than inside a package on purpose: it belongs to no framework. It says what the component IS — its purpose, its behaviour, the states it must be able to show, the axes it exposes, its anatomy, and which family of token paints each part. It does NOT say how any of that is expressed in React, or in React Native, or in a web component. That is a binding, and bindings live beside the implementation.

Buildable means: someone handed this file, the prop map for their framework, and the code standards should be able to produce the component without asking what it is for.

component.description: PascalCase name. Tooling asserts it matches the directory and, in each binding, the implementation.

status.description: Lifecycle. Structured rather than a bare string, so a deprecation cannot exist without somewhere to migrate to.

intent.description:
WHY this component exists, and what it must do. This is the written form of the use case — the thinking a designer does before an API can be laid out at all. Without it the anatomy below is someone's opinion rather than a consequence.

It is also the half no extraction, no linter and no schema can ever check. It is here because a component whose purpose is not written down gets re-litigated every time somebody new looks at it.

purpose.description: One or two sentences. What job does this do that nothing else does? A purpose that would equally describe three other components in the library means the boundary is wrong.

behaviour.description: What it does in response to use, in plain language. Interaction model, keyboard model, what happens on activation, what it does NOT do. This is what makes the file buildable rather than merely descriptive.

notFor.description: Uses this component deliberately does not cover, and what to reach for instead. The section that stops the component being quietly widened until it means nothing.

states.description:
Every state this component must be able to REPRESENT, keyed by name. Distinct from the per-part paint overrides in `anatomy`: this is the declaration that the state exists at all and where it comes from, so a design can be checked against it before any styling is written.

`intrinsic` — the platform provides it (hover, focus, pressed, disabled). You do not implement it, you only style it.
`authored`  — someone sets it (loading, current, selected). The implementation has to track it.

values.description:
The values this state may hold, in a meaningful order. EXPERIMENTAL.

OMIT IT AND THE STATE IS A BOOLEAN, which is what every state in this schema was until a checkbox needed three conditions — unchecked, checked and mixed. Two booleans cannot carry that: `checked` and `indeterminate` as separate flags admits `checked: true, indeterminate: true`, which is meaningless, and no gate here could reject it.

Not the same thing as an `axis`. An axis is a styling choice the consumer makes; a state is a condition the component is in, and may be set by the platform or derived.

default.description: The value before anything sets one. Only meaningful alongside `values`, and must be one of them.

valueType.description:
For a state whose value CANNOT BE LISTED. EXPERIMENTAL.

The three shapes a state may take, and how to say each:
  say nothing        -> a boolean. Most states.
  `values: [...]`    -> one of a fixed set. A checkbox's unchecked/checked/mixed.
  `valueType`        -> free text, or a number in a range. A text field, a slider.

Added because a text field's value is not a boolean and cannot be enumerated, and a slider's is a number with bounds. Both were previously inexpressible, which meant the two most common controls in any library could not be described at all.

min.description: Smallest permitted value. Only with `valueType: number`. A slider's range lives nowhere else — not in an axis, which is a styling choice, and not in `values`, which cannot enumerate a continuum.

max.description: Largest permitted value. Only with `valueType: number`.

step.description: The granularity of movement. Only with `valueType: number`. A value between steps is not reachable, which is a promise a consumer relies on.

control.description:
WHO MAY SET THIS STATE. Distinct from `kind`, which says who TRACKS it — the two are orthogonal, and `disabled` proves it: the platform tracks it (intrinsic) but only the consumer sets it (consumer).

This is the bit a framework binding compiles into a public surface, and it is the reason this file can be translated rather than merely read:
  `consumer` -> the consumer sets it; the user cannot change it. Compiles to ONE input.        e.g. disabled
  `shared`   -> the consumer may set it AND the user may change it. Compiles to whatever that framework uses for two-way state — in React a controlled/uncontrolled trio, in Vue a v-model pair.   e.g. checked, open
  `internal` -> nothing outside sets it: the platform observes it, the component derives it, or an ancestor owns it. Compiles to NO input at all.   e.g. hover, focus-visible, an accordion item's open state

Deliberately says nothing about prop names. `checked` + `defaultChecked` + `onCheckedChange` is React's SPELLING of `shared`; Vue spells the same fact `modelValue` + `update:modelValue`. Naming either here would put a framework in an agnostic file. Each framework's spelling is a RULE in its own prop-bindings.json, which is why one rule covers every shared state in the library rather than one entry per component.

visual.description:
What must visibly change, where anything does. Most states paint something, and one that paints nothing is worth questioning hard.

But not all of them do, and the earlier form of this rule — 'a state nobody can see is not a state' — was measured to be wrong. A GATING state like `touched` or `dirty` exists to decide WHEN another state may display; it is real, the implementation must track it, and it honestly paints nothing. Say so plainly rather than inventing a treatment to fill the field. Whether such states deserve a `kind` of their own is open — see docs/research/0001-contract-schema-smoke-test.md.

axes.description:
The canonical axes this component exposes, and the SUBSET of values it takes. Axis names and their canonical values come from the prop map — a component narrows an axis, it never invents a value.

This is specified here, and the implementation also expresses it. That duplication is deliberate and safe, because a gate asserts the two are equal. It is what makes the contract something you can build FROM rather than only describe with.

values.description: A subset of the axis's canonical values, in canonical order.

semantics.description: What the component MEANS. Deliberately not what element it renders — that is a binding concern, because `button` and `Pressable` are the same meaning in two frameworks.

role.description: The semantic role, e.g. `button`, `link`, `listitem`. Each binding maps this to whatever its platform uses (an HTML element, an accessibilityRole, an ARIA attribute).

roleByAxis.description: For components whose meaning changes with an axis value.

focusable.description: Whether this takes a place in the focus order at all.

a11y.description: Accessibility commitments. Not checkable — a wrong role or an optimistic contrast claim passes every gate — so write it as a statement of intent a human reviews.

minHitArea.description: CSS px. 44 for WCAG 2.5.5 AAA, 24 for 2.5.8 AA.

keyboard.description: One line on the keyboard model.

notes.description: Prefer naming what the component CANNOT enforce. That is the fact nothing else records.

collection.description:
This component holds a SELECTION across a set of children — which tab is current, which accordion sections are open, which options are chosen. EXPERIMENTAL: added to find out whether an accordion can be compiled at all; not yet recorded in an ADR.

Declared here rather than as a `state` because a state is a boolean this component is IN, and a selection is a set of identities this component HOLDS. The children declare the other half with `member`.

items.description:
The component, or components, that may be a member. Each must name a real contract.

AN ARRAY BECAUSE A SELECTION CAN HAVE MORE THAN ONE KIND OF MEMBER. A tab strip's selection is read by both the tab and its panel: the tab shows it is chosen, the panel shows itself. Both compare against the same value and both are members, and a single name could only admit one of them.

identity.description: What distinguishes one member from another. A NAME, not a prop: each binding spells it in its own vocabulary.

cardinality.description: `one` — exactly one is always selected; a tab list can never show nothing. `at-most-one` — zero or one; a single-open accordion may close its last section. `many` — any number. Collapsing the first two into a boolean `multiple` loses a real distinction.

control.description: Same three values as a state's `control`, and the same meaning. A binding compiles them the same way.

initial.description: What is selected before anyone chooses. Omitted means undecided, not `none`.

navigation.description:
How a user moves between this collection's members with the keyboard. EXPERIMENTAL.

A named primitive with named parameters, never a key map. Every parameter below corresponds to something the W3C ARIA APG states about the radio-group and tabs patterns, and the cases a backend must satisfy are transcribed as data in packages/contracts/conformance/linear-navigation.json. The specification work is citation, not invention.

Declaring this block also declares the composite's focus behaviour: exactly one member sits in the page's tab sequence, so Tab enters the collection and then leaves it. HOW that is achieved — a roving tabindex, or aria-activedescendant — is a backend's choice and deliberately not stated here. The APG demonstrates both for radio groups and states no preference; the conformance cases assert the OUTCOME, one tab stop, not the technique.

orientation.description:
Which arrow keys move between members. Vocabulary from prop-canon.json, which is also what aria-orientation takes.

THIS DECIDES A NEGATIVE REQUIREMENT, not just a positive one. A `horizontal` collection must LEAVE Up and Down alone — the APG is explicit that a horizontal tab list "does not listen for Down Arrow or Up Arrow so those keys can provide their normal browser scrolling functions even when focus is inside the tab list". Consuming a key you were told not to handle breaks page scrolling for a keyboard user.

`both` is not a convenience. A radio group answers all four arrows regardless of how it is laid out — the APG groups "Right Arrow and Down Arrow" in a single bullet, as strict equivalents — and never mentions aria-orientation on that pattern at all.

wrap.description:
Whether moving past the last member returns to the first, and vice versa. Unmarked — therefore stated unconditionally — in both patterns the APG describes.

Worth noticing where the APG put its marker: in the tabs pattern the wrap clause and an explicitly optional activation clause sit in the SAME sentence, and only one of them is marked. That contrast is deliberate.

followsFocus.description:
Whether moving focus also changes the selection.

For a radio group this is not a choice: the APG writes it into the arrow key's own definition — the keys "move focus to the next radio button in the group, uncheck the previously focused button, and check the newly focused button". A radio group whose arrows move without checking is not implementing the pattern.

For a tab list it is explicitly optional, and the APG gives the deciding criterion: automatic where a panel is already in the DOM, manual where displaying one causes a network request or a page refresh. Its threshold phrase is "noticeable latency".

When false, activation moves to the member's own `activates` — a native button already answers Space and Enter, which is exactly what the APG asks for: "Activates the tab if it was not activated automatically on focus."

disabledItems.description:
What arrow navigation does when it reaches a disabled member. NOT A BOOLEAN, because the two patterns the APG describes want opposite answers and it is a real trade rather than an oversight.

`focusable` — the member keeps its place in the arrow path and is marked disabled for assistive technology. This is the APG's own convention and it names tabs explicitly: "aria-disabled='true' is applied so that it will remain focusable ... Tab elements in a set of Tabs". Its reasoning is that "screen reader users are far less likely to discover disabled elements that are not focusable because moving focus is one of their primary methods of discovery".

`skip` — navigation passes over it. Fewer key presses, and the cost is that a keyboard user cannot land on the member to find out it exists and is unavailable. The radio pattern page never mentions disabled items and radio buttons are absent from the APG's stay-focusable list, so choosing `skip` there is OUR decision and the contract should say so in its a11y notes.

homeEnd.description: Whether Home and End jump to the first and last member. Marked `(Optional)` by the APG for tabs, and not addressed at all for radio groups — the radio pattern lists no Home or End key. Omit it rather than assume it.

member.description:
This component is a member of an ancestor's `collection`. EXPERIMENTAL, as above.

It is the other half of `collection`: the ancestor owns the selection, and this says how a member finds out whether it is in it.

of.description: The ancestor holding the collection. Must match that contract's `collection.items`.

identity.description: This member's own identity. Must match the ancestor's `collection.identity`.

reflects.description: Which of THIS component's states is true when it is in the selection. That state must be declared with `control: internal` — the ancestor owns it, so no framework may expose an input for it.

range.description:
This component is OPERATED as a number in a range: a slider, a progress-setter, a zoom control. EXPERIMENTAL.

The range itself — `min`, `max`, `step` — already lives on the state, because those are facts about the VALUE. This block says how a person moves it, which is a different question and the one no contract could previously answer. It is the sibling of `collection.navigation`: named parameters only, no expressions, and every field maps to a case in `packages/contracts/conformance/range-stepping.json`.

Naming a `track` is what makes dragging expressible at all. A pointer position is meaningless until something says which box it is measured against, and that box is a part of this component's anatomy — so the contract can state it without knowing anything about pixels, events or a rendering model.

state.description: The state this operates. It must be declared in `states` with `valueType: "number"`, and its `min`, `max` and `step` are the range.

track.description: The part whose extent is the full range. A pointer's position is measured against this part's box: its start is the minimum and its end is the maximum. `root` is legal and is the usual answer when the track is drawn edge to edge.

orientation.description: Which way the value increases: along the inline axis, or up the block axis. This governs the POINTER only. All four arrow keys move a slider whatever its orientation — the APG says so plainly, and it is the opposite of the rule for a tab list.

pageStep.description: How far Page Up and Page Down move. The APG marks these keys Optional, so OMITTING this field is a real answer: the keys are then left alone and scroll the page. A range of 0–100 stepping by 1 is a hundred presses end to end, which is conformant and unusable, and this is the field that fixes it.

drag.description: Whether a pointer press and drag along the track sets the value. The APG specifies no pointer behaviour for a slider at all, so this is not a conformance requirement — it is this system stating an affordance the specification declines to describe.

dismisses.description:
What CLOSES this component, by a key or a press that is NOT activation. EXPERIMENTAL.

The sibling of `range` and `collection.navigation`: a named primitive with named parameters, never a key map. The cases a backend must satisfy are in packages/contracts/conformance/dismissal.json.

IT RESTS ON WEAKER GROUND THAN THE OTHER TWO, and that is worth knowing before relying on it. The APG's tooltip pattern is explicitly a work in progress without task force consensus — it states that Escape dismisses and never states what shows a tooltip — and the APG says nothing at all about pressing a backdrop. So one cause is a citation from an unsettled page and the other is entirely ours. Both are marked as such in the conformance file.

Dismissal is deliberately separate from `activates`. Activation is a thing a person does TO a control and it belongs to the control; dismissal is a thing that happens to a REGION and it belongs to the region. Folding Escape into `activates` would make every activatable part a candidate for closing its own ancestor.

state.description: The state that becomes false. It must be declared in `states` with `control: "shared"` — a dismissal writes it, so something outside has to be able to hear that.

on.description:
The causes, as a SET rather than a choice — declaring both does not make either conditional on the other.

`escape` — the Escape key, from anywhere inside the region.

`outside-press` — a press that lands on the REGION ITSELF rather than on any descendant. That phrasing is precise and measured rather than loose: a native `<dialog>`'s backdrop is a pseudo-element and is never an event target, so a press on it reports the dialog as the target. The same test — target is the region, not something inside it — also describes a hand-rolled scrim wrapping a panel.

IT DOES NOT MEAN a press elsewhere on the page. That needs a document-level listener and a portalled component to be worth having, and nothing in this system is portalled. A backend MAY implement it that way; the cases assert the outcome, not the mechanism.

A cause left out is a real answer: a component that declares only `escape` must not acquire a press it never asked for.

composition.description: What may be placed inside. Frameworks differ on the mechanism (children, slots, render props); they agree on the constraint.

anatomy.description: The tree of named pieces, and the token policy for each. Agnostic: a piece is a named region with a job, not a div.

part.description:
Which anatomy part this slot's content fills. EXPERIMENTAL.

Without it, a slot and a part are two vocabularies for the same place and nothing reconciles them: a slot whose name happens to match a part key worked by luck, and one that did not — a field's `control`, an accordion item's `heading` — rendered outside any described region, in declaration order, which put a form control below its own error message.

max.description: 0 is legal and means the component accepts nothing here. A switch's label is a sibling it is associated with, not a child it contains — `max: 0` says that outright, where an empty `accepts` list only says 'none of these'.

tokenPolicyAtom.description: One permitted source for a visual channel — a namespace PREFIX, never a value. The concrete prefix comes from /ds.config.json.

tokenPolicy.description:
Where this channel's value may come from — or `null`, meaning the library deliberately does not say.

THE UNSTYLED DEFAULT IS `null`. This library ships no visual opinion, so a contract names the channel a part paints and leaves the source unbound for a consumer to wire. Read it as a patch bay: the contract says this part has a socket for a block-end border, not what to plug in. Deleting the channel instead would leave a consumer nothing to wire and force them to reverse-engineer a stylesheet, which is the failure this library exists to remove.

Two notations, two different facts, and conflating them loses the distinction:
  `"channel": null`   -> UNBOUND BY DESIGN. The consumer supplies this.
  channel omitted     -> NOT DESCRIBED YET. Nobody has established what it paints.

A named policy is still legal and is what a consumer's own wiring, or a reference implementation like @ds/tokens, would state. Prefer group-less role families (--ds-color-fill-, --ds-color-border-, --ds-color-on-): those are what a variant axis re-points, so a component styled against them gets every variant free. Naming a branded family pins it to one colour.

`literal` means a deliberate non-token value and always wants a reason. An ARRAY is a permitted SET, not a preference — a border that is transparent at rest and a token when outlined declares both.

paints.description:
Visual channel -> token policy. Not exhaustive: list what carries design intent (colour, spacing, radius, type, elevation, motion), not every layout declaration.

STRUCTURAL CHANNELS ARE REJECTED. `display`, `position`, the inset properties, the flex and grid properties and their friends are layout, not paint, and a consumer's theme file is the wrong home for them: delete that file and a component with structure in it does not become unstyled, it becomes BROKEN. Two contracts had already put `display` here before this was enforced.

Spacing stays — `gap`, `padding` and `margin` carry design intent and belong to the token system. So does sizing. The line is: does it decide WHERE something sits, or how it LOOKS?

whenAxis.description: Paint overrides driven by an AXIS VALUE rather than a state, keyed `axis=value` or a bare boolean axis name. Every key must name an axis declared above, and its value must be one this component actually takes — which is checkable precisely because `axes` declares them.

part.description: One named region of the component.
kebab-case name. Each binding exposes this to consumers in whatever way its platform allows; in React that is a data attribute.

internalOnly.description: Structural, deliberately not exposed to consumers. Recording it says the omission was a decision.

role.description:
The semantic role of THIS part, where it is not the root's. EXPERIMENTAL.

Top-level `semantics.role` is the root's role, which is wrong whenever the meaning belongs to an inner region: an accordion item's `button` belongs to its trigger, and putting it on the root makes the whole section — heading and panel together — announce as one control.

activates.description:
What happens when a user activates this part — clicks it, or presses Enter or Space on it. EXPERIMENTAL.

Deliberately NOT a general effect list. It takes one named thing, because the moment it takes an expression this schema has become a programming language.

toggles.description: A state name declared in `states`, or the literal `member` meaning this component's membership of its ancestor's collection.

between.description:
For a state with more than two values: the two a USER may move between, and the resting one to fall back to from any other. EXPERIMENTAL.

A checkbox holds three values and a user may only reach two of them: `mixed` is reported by a parent whose children disagree, and activating a mixed checkbox resolves it to checked. Without this, activation would have to guess — and offering `mixed` as a third click target is a real defect in real libraries.

Required when the toggled state declares more than two values.

controls.description:
Names another part whose presence or visibility this part governs. Compiles to `aria-controls` on the web. EXPERIMENTAL.

A plain string names a part of this same component. The object form crosses to a sibling member of the same collection — the reference a tab makes to its panel, which no sibling-only form could express: a tab and its panel are different components that share one collection and one identity.

member.description: The sibling MEMBER KIND holding the referenced part. It must be a component the shared ancestor admits in `collection.items`, and both members must carry the same `member.identity` — that identity is what pairs one tab with one panel. Naming a component here is no more coupling than `member.of` already is: it is a contract name, not a framework one.

part.description: The part within that member. `root` names the member's own outermost node.

oneOf.description: A part of a sibling member of the same collection.

namedBy.description:
Names another part that supplies this one's accessible name. Compiles to `aria-labelledby` on the web, `accessibilityLabelledBy` elsewhere. EXPERIMENTAL.

A plain string names a part of this same component; the object form crosses to a sibling member of the same collection, which is how a tab panel is named by its tab. This and `describedBy` are the fields whose absence made the generated Field render four correct regions that knew nothing about each other.

member.description: The sibling MEMBER KIND holding the referenced part. It must be a component the shared ancestor admits in `collection.items`, and both members must carry the same `member.identity` — that identity is what pairs one tab with one panel. Naming a component here is no more coupling than `member.of` already is: it is a contract name, not a framework one.

part.description: The part within that member. `root` names the member's own outermost node.

oneOf.description: A part of a sibling member of the same collection.

describedBy.description: Names other parts that supply this one's supplementary description, IN ANNOUNCEMENT ORDER. An array because a field's help text and its error are both descriptions and their order is not incidental. EXPERIMENTAL.

visibleWhen.description:
Names a state; this part is hidden whenever that state is false. For a state with `values`, write `state=value` — a checkbox's tick is `checked=checked` and its dash is `checked=mixed`, two different marks for two different facts rather than one mark shown twice. EXPERIMENTAL.

Hidden, not removed: the part stays in the document so find-in-page can reach it and so anything measured inside it survives. A component that must unmount its hidden content is a different decision and has no home here yet.

backdrop.description:
The obscuring layer this part draws over everything behind it while it is showing. EXPERIMENTAL.

Declared here rather than as a child part because on some platforms it IS NOT ONE. A native `<dialog>` renders its backdrop as a pseudo-element: it can be painted, and it can never hold a child, carry an attribute, or be the target of an event. A contract that modelled it as a part would be promising three things the platform cannot give.

So this says only what is true everywhere: there is a layer, it belongs to this part, and these are its paint channels. A backend that has a real element for it may render one; a backend that gets it from the platform styles what the platform gives.

states.description: Per-state paint overrides. Every key must be declared in the top-level `states`, so styling cannot describe a state the component does not have.
